turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Before you head in, his blood pressure was 148 over 86, pulse 78, and the finger-prick was 11.2 millimoles. He told me he's on 18 units of Lantus at night, but he was a bit vague, so I'd check it.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta for that. Mr Callahan, come through. What's been the trouble?

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): G'day doc. It's the sugars, they've been rotten the last few weeks. Work's gone mad, new supervisor at the warehouse has us starting at five, and the kelpie's up half the night barking at possums, so I'm wrecked before I even clock on.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possums can wait. When you say rotten, what sort of numbers are you getting at home?

[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Fasting's been, um, one-eighty-something. I look at the meter, think yep not flash, and carry on. I was meant to write them in that little book. It's in a drawer under the phone charger, I think.

[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): One-eighty-something... that meter's still talking American, I suspect. In millimoles that'd sit somewhere near ten, but the something means I can't treat it as a real figure. What are you taking for the diabetes?

[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Metformin for the diabetes, those big tablets, a thousand milligrams morning and night. Lantus as well, twelve units, I inject it before bed. I've had the type 2 about eight years.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, can I jump in. The last script, the one dispensed at the chemist back in March, says insulin glargine 18 units at night. Not twelve.

[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll tell you twelve till he's blue in the face. I'm his wife, I collect the repeats. And on early shifts that pen does not leave the fridge. He reckons he'll do it when he gets home, then it's late arvo and he's forgotten.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so on those work days the night dose just doesn't happen?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. If I'm on an early I often skip it. Maybe three mornings a week. Nights, I mean. The injection's at night, except those ones. I know that's not brilliant.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's check the feet. Any numbness, tingling, sores?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Nah, feet are fine. I'm walking the warehouse floor all day, they'd let me know.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the eyes? Any blurring, any floaters, and have you had the diabetic photo this year?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Eyes are good, no blurring. Haven't done the photo since before the lockdowns. I walk past the optometrist near the servo and just... don't go in.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of.

[SEG0018] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hang on, he was complaining about his big toe the other night, during the footy. Said it was buzzing. You can't tell the doctor your feet are fine and then say that to me.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. So something is going on in the feet. What exactly have you noticed?

[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah. The right big toe tingles at night, been a couple of weeks. And there's a little split on the heel, dry, not really sore. I didn't think it counted. New steel caps, probably.

[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): It counts. Both foot pulses are easy to feel. There's a shallow fissure on the right heel, dry, no redness, no pus. Sensation in that right big toe is duller than the left.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): See, the boots. Bloke on my shift says steel caps always do your heels in. They're also rostering us over the grand final weekend, which is a bit rough if you ask me.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud here. Clinic sugar is 11.2, home readings sound high, so my usual move would be to put the Lantus up to 22 units every night and see you in a month.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If you give him a new number on top of the 12 versus 18 mess, and he still skips the work nights, he'll get in a tangle. I won't know what to set the pen to.

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yeah. Fair cop. Scratch the increase. I'm not changing the dose today, not while we can't agree if it's 12 or 18, and not while doses are being missed. Forget the month-away plan as well.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): So I just keep doing what I'm doing?

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): You use the insulin on the current script, every night, including the nights before an early start. Do it before you leave the house if you have to, but don't skip it. Metformin stays a thousand milligrams morning and night. And take the box to the chemist, get them to write down whether the script says 12 or 18, and bring that note with you.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): What I will do is order an HbA1c today, urea and electrolytes, and a urine albumin, so we've got the longer-term sugar and a look at the kidneys. I'm also referring you to the high-risk foot clinic for that heel and the dull sensation, rather than just keeping an eye on it myself. And I'll send a referral for diabetic eye screening, because that photo is well overdue.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, I'd say the diabetes isn't well controlled just now, and the tingling plus the dull feeling is probably early nerve change from the diabetes. That's provisional, mind you, not a final label. The heel itself doesn't look infected.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Righto. Doing the insulin before I walk out means even less sleep. The kelpie already thinks five o'clock is breakfast. Vet says we're spoiling her, which, yeah, we are.
[SEG0031] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll park the pen next to his keys. And I'll get him to those appointments, otherwise they'll slide.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks with the chemist's note and any numbers you manage to write down. If the heel turns red, hot, or starts oozing before that, come straight in, don't wait for the fortnight.

[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks, yep. The meter will still say that one-eighty business. My brother-in-law set it up, and he spends half the year in the States, so that explains a bit. I might get a coffee on the way if the machine downstairs is working.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't fight the meter today. Just write whatever number you see, and the time, and we'll make sense of it here. Anything else going on, thirst, getting up at night to wee?

[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Thirsty, a bit, yeah, especially of an arvo. Not more than usual for the loo. Otherwise I'm alright. The coffee machine's been broken all week anyway, so that's that tangent dead.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take you for the bloods now. Reception will book the foot clinic and the eye screening, and I'll lock in the two-week visit once I've got a slot.
